questions.text: In off-policy Monte Carlo evaluation, why are importance-sampling weights needed?

options.A: They convert a full episode return into an immediate reward.
options.B: They correct for trajectories sampled under a behavior policy different from the target policy.
options.C: They replace exploration with exact model-based expectations.
options.D: They make the next-state value estimate stationary during training.

questions.explanation: Off-policy data comes from behavior policy μ, while the target is π. Importance weights use their action-probability ratios to account for that difference.

questions.text: Off-policy Monte Carlo importance weights become extremely variable on long episodes because action-probability ratios multiply across steps. Which response does the lesson recommend?

options.A: Use a per-decision weighted importance-sampling variant or switch to TD.
options.B: Increase the episode horizon so the ratio product averages out.
options.C: Drop importance weights while still evaluating the target policy from behavior-policy data.
options.D: Set every action probability under the target policy to one.

questions.explanation: The lesson flags exploding trajectory-weight variance and recommends per-decision weighted importance sampling or a TD method.

questions.text: In mc_control, seen stores (state, action) pairs. An episode visits (s,left), then (s,right), then (s,left), with following returns 5, 4, and 3. Which returns update Q in this episode?

options.A: Only 5, because s is counted once regardless of action.
options.B: 5 and 4, because the repeated (s,left) pair is skipped.
options.C: 5 and 3, because the first and last actions match.
options.D: 5, 4, and 3, because all visits are counted.

questions.explanation: The first (s,left) and first (s,right) are distinct pairs and both update Q. The second (s,left) is already in seen, so its return 3 is skipped.
